section_summary: This section concludes “A Survey of Japanese News Agencies,” describing general, labor, commercial, cultural, photographic, and repatriation-oriented services, followed by agency directories, an English-name index, sources, and interview records. The remaining documents concern requests for information about the Japanese press, wire-service payment arrangements, newspaper mergers, enforcement of the occupation Press Code, General MacArthur’s statement for National Newspaper Week, and the circulation of Japanese newspapers domestically and abroad. Together they document the structure, politics, regulation, and postwar democratization of Japan’s press between 1945 and 1949.

subfiles.title: A Survey of Japanese News Agencies: concluding chapters, appendices, index, sources, and conferences
subfiles.from: Information Media Research, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Surveys the organization, ownership, politics, circulation, and operations of Japanese news agencies and supplies reference appendices and sources.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion begins in the report's chapter on general agencies and then examines labor, business, commercial, cultural, repatriation, Chinese-language, and photographic news services. It records agency histories, ownership, staffing, subscription figures, editorial positions, wartime experiences, and relationships with SCAP, political parties, unions, and commercial interests. Appendices list agency names and addresses, provide an English-name index, and document the reports, publications, and interviews used as sources.

subfiles.title: Walter Leifer's request for information about the Japanese press
subfiles.about: Requests statistics, historical information, and sample publications concerning journalism and newspapers in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: German journalist Walter Leifer asks about Japanese newspapers' numbers, circulation, licensing and postwar development, especially Roman-alphabet papers, and for titles and samples, naming Rev. Leopold Jibeser as a contact.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on charges for press-wire news services in Japan
subfiles.about: Reviews proposed currency arrangements for Japanese payments to international press-wire services.
subfiles.summary: OFD memo: SCAP proposes the Japanese share of news-service charges be paid wholly in yen while Draper contemplates 25 percent in dollars; OFD finds it of limited importance and will concur with Draper.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 21: Anticipated Reorganization in Japanese Newspaper Field
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports prospective changes in Kyodo's relationship with major newspapers and mergers among Tokyo afternoon papers.
subfiles.summary: Sebald: Mainichi and Asahi may leave Kyodo, using little of its material; major chains expand into Tokyo's afternoon market through subsidiaries and Tokyo Mimpo's paper allocation; one trade paper questions an Anti-Monopoly Law violation.

subfiles.title: Incoming airgram permanent-record sheet
subfiles.about: Records the routing and filing of an incoming airgram under the Japanese press decimal-file classification.
subfiles.summary: Largely blank permanent-record form for an incoming airgram.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-246 on enforcement of the occupation Press Code
subfiles.about: Reports prosecutions for Press Code violations and the creation of machinery for reviewing alleged offenses.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-246: degraded report of Army provost-court cases for Press Code violations, often against alleged Communist sympathizers, following a policy decision and a review committee.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 684 and enclosures: General MacArthur's Statement on National Newspaper Week in Japan
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits copies of General MacArthur's statement praising the development and responsibilities of Japan's postwar free press.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 684: MacArthur's statement for National Newspaper Week praises the press's move from despotic control to freedom and urges publishers to use it for truth, law and order; duplicates included.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-207 requesting a survey of leading Japanese newspapers
subfiles.from: Department of State, James E. Webb acting
subfiles.about: Requests a summary of the policies, party affiliations, circulation, and influence of leading Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-207 asks the mission for a survey of leading Japanese newspapers after requests such as the Council on Foreign Relations' Political Handbook of the World.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 106: Transmission of Japanese Newspapers for Distribution to Japanese Colonies in South America
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards post-surrender Tokyo newspapers for distribution among Japanese communities in Brazil and Peru.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson sends Tokyo newspapers for Japanese communities in Brazil, recommending some go to Lima, as they show Japan's defeat and democratization.
